catalog_quote: The syllables of Mi'gmaq can be roughly classified into two types: heavy and light. Heavy syllables are those which contain a long vowel or a coda consonant (Barkhouse 1998); light syllables contain a short vowel. [...] By looking at the data in (7), repeated below (with some additional forms) in (9), it can be seen that (1) all heavy syllables receive stress, (2) the first syllable receives stress, (3) every second light vowel in a sequence of light vowels (counting from right to left) receives stress, and (4) primary stress falls on the rightmost stressed syllable. [...] (10) Stress assignment in Listuguj Mi'gmaq a. Build moraically binary trochees. b. Build feet from right to left. c. Allow degenerate feet. d. Place primary stress on the rightmost stressed syllable. [...] It has been shown that Mi'gmaq assigns accent to the heads of bimoraic trochees, with the rightmost stress being the primary stress. [...] Mi'gmaq forms feet from right to left and also allows degenerate feet. Syllables containing long vowels and those containing coda consonants are heavy (or bimoraic), while all others are light (or monomoraic), so that heavy syllables will always receive stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive: heavy syllables (long vowel or closed by a coda consonant) are always stressed; light (short open) syllables are parsed into moraic trochees from the right edge, with the word-initial syllable always stressed (degenerate feet allowed); the rightmost stress in the word is primary. In practice primary stress falls on the final syllable when it is heavy (and, in isolation/citation forms, also when it ends in a short vowel, which then behaves as heavy), otherwise on the rightmost foot head further left. Main acoustic correlate is amplitude; the primary-stressed syllable also carries higher pitch (possibly phrasal).
new_statements.secondary_stress: All non-rightmost foot heads carry secondary stress: every heavy syllable, every second light syllable counting right-to-left, and the word-initial syllable. Optional clash resolution: when two stresses are adjacent and the second is on a light syllable it may be deleted (common in connected/relaxed speech), or word-initially the leftmost clash member is strengthened.
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final short vowels count as heavy (stressed) in isolation but not phrase-medially ('phrase-final strengthening', p.277); schwa is often 'invisible' (non-moraic) to stress, but becomes visible when it is the first or last vowel of the word, after a consonant cluster, or when lexically specified (pp.278-281); CəC syllables count as light; non-bound preverbs form their own stress domain (wiki version). Author notes transcription was by ear for most data and that phrasal behaviour remains to be studied. Earlier, vaguer statements: Fidelholtz 1968:29 'second mora from the end of the word (perhaps not counting a final short syllable) seems to get stress'; Bragg 1976:37-38 stress non-distinctive in Newfoundland Micmac, long vowels attract stress with alternating secondaries.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress of citation forms (words spoken in isolation from the Mi'gmaq Talking Dictionary, Listuguj speakers); Olson explicitly flags that final-light-syllable stress and the H pitch on primary stress may be phrase-final/intonational effects; stress is not contrastive (Bragg 1976; vowel length is contrastive instead).
new_statements.identity_note: Olson 2012 describes the Listuguj (Restigouche, Quebec) dialect of Mi'gmaq specifically (speakers aged 40-50+, Mi'gmaq Talking Dictionary recordings); Glottolog treats Mi'kmaq mikm1235 as a single language without dialect glottocodes. Bragg 1976 and Steeves 2022 describe Newfoundland (Conne River) Micmac; Fidelholtz 1968 data are mainly from Restigouche as well. All fall under mikm1235.

sources.note: Learner-oriented restatement of Olson 2012: stress every heavy syllable; every second light syllable R-to-L; first syllable always stressed; last stressed syllable = primary; word-final short vowel counts as heavy; optional clash deletion in conversational speech; schwa usually weightless/invisible; only primary-stressed syllable has higher pitch.
